findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the claim that the happy-path stderr assertion catches a never-disarmed trap with a test that actually does: make the script exit after a successful SSM write but before step 5's `trap ... EXIT` line, then assert the notice is absent.
evidence: Plan: 'assert "already replaced" is absent from stderr on a successful run, which catches a trap that is never disarmed.'
infra/gerrit/service-user.sh:89-90: `work="$(mktemp -d)"` / `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT` replaces the EXIT trap unconditionally.
tests/scripts/test_operator_credential_argv.py:77: git stub `diff) exit 1 ;;`, so the happy path always reaches step 5's commit/push and the replacement trap.
findings.finding: The plan claims the new 'already replaced is absent' assertion in the happy-path test 'catches a trap that is never disarmed'. It cannot. Step 5 of service-user.sh runs `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT`, which replaces any EXIT trap still armed, and the stubbed happy path always reaches step 5 because the git stub's `diff` exits 1. If `trap - EXIT` were left out, that test would still pass, so the regression it is meant to catch goes undetected.
findings.location: Testing — edit to `test_service_user_keeps_the_token_out_of_every_argv`; Approach — 'Disarmed with `trap - EXIT` ... before step 5 installs its own cleanup trap'
scenarios: A later edit drops or moves the `trap - EXIT` line. The happy-path test still passes because line 90 overwrites the trap. A failure between the SSM write and line 90, such as `mktemp -d` failing, would then wrongly print 'SSM was NOT updated' after SSM was in fact written.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a test where the `aws` stub succeeds and the script then fails before line 90. For example, put a `mktemp` stub on PATH that exits 1, then assert a non-zero exit and that 'already replaced' is NOT in stderr. Keep the happy-path assertion as a general regression check, but stop describing it as the guard against a missing disarm.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Account for bash running the EXIT trap on fatal signals: make the trap print the definite 'SSM was NOT updated' notice only for ordinary non-zero exits, and print an 'SSM state unknown, verify or re-run' message (or nothing) when the exit status is >128. Correct the Root cause/Approach text that says signals run no code.
evidence: Plan: 'No signals handlers are added: ... a signal during the `aws` write leaves the SSM state unknowable from the script.'
Plan: 'every other way out between the delete and the SSM write is an implicit `set -e` exit or a signal, which runs no code.'
Plan: 'The trap window matches the facts the notice states'
infra/gerrit/service-user.sh:77-83: the SSM write is a foreground pipeline. Per the plan, the disarm comes only after it returns successfully.
findings.finding: The plan says no signal handlers are needed because a signal 'runs no code' and 'leaves the SSM state unknowable', but bash runs an EXIT trap when the shell is terminated by a fatal signal (SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGHUP). With the trap armed, a signal during or just after `aws ssm put-parameter` will print 'SSM was NOT updated'. That claim can be false. bash defers a SIGTERM aimed at the script until the foreground `aws` child finishes, so the write may already have succeeded before the shell dies and runs the still-armed trap, ahead of the `trap - EXIT` line. So the trap window does not actually 'match the facts the notice states' for signal exits, and the Root cause claim that a signal 'runs no code' stops being true once the EXIT trap exists.
findings.location: Approach (EXIT trap / 'No signal handlers are added'); Root cause ('or a signal, which runs no code')
scenarios: An operator presses Ctrl-C, or a CI timeout sends SIGTERM, while `aws ssm put-parameter` is running. The write completes on AWS, bash then dies of the pending signal, and the armed EXIT trap prints 'SSM was NOT updated'. The operator re-runs and rotates the token again, or debugs a lockout that never happened.
A SIGHUP from a dropped terminal during the generator call prints the lockout notice even though the generator's outcome is unknown.
findings.suggested_fix: In the trap body, capture `rc=$?` first. If `rc` is greater than 128 (killed by a signal), print a hedged line such as "service-user: interrupted after Gerrit's token for '$BOT_USER' may have been replaced; SSM state unknown — re-run this script". Otherwise print the definite notice. Then fix the plan's Root cause/Approach wording so it no longer says signals run no code under an EXIT trap.

findings.finding: The plan says signals are out of scope and adds no signal handlers. But bash runs an armed EXIT trap when the shell is killed by a fatal signal such as SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP, unlike dash. So once the trap is armed, the SIGTERM-during-`aws` case from Root cause will print "SSM was NOT updated". That is the state the plan itself calls 'unknowable'. Worse: a SIGTERM that arrives while bash waits on a successful `aws ssm put-parameter` is handled before `trap - EXIT` runs. The notice would then falsely claim SSM was not updated.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Check (by stub reproduction) whether bash runs the planned EXIT trap on SIGTERM/SIGINT during the `aws` write, and either reword the notice for an unknown SSM state, disarm or suppress it on signals, or explicitly accept and document the behaviour, adding a test for whichever you choose.
evidence: Plan Root cause: 'every other way out between the delete and the SSM write is an implicit `set -e` exit or a signal, which runs no code.' This holds only for today's script, which has no EXIT trap in that window.
Plan Approach: the trap is armed from the delete or generator through the `aws` call and disarmed only after `aws ssm put-parameter` succeeds, so it is armed throughout the SSM write.
The plan reproduced a SIGTERM during `aws` (rc 143) against the unfixed script but never re-checks that case once the planned EXIT trap exists, and none of its tests covers it.
The plan offers no Grep/Read or reproduction showing that an EXIT trap stays silent on SIGTERM or SIGINT under bash; per E4 an unverified premise is a gap.
findings.finding: The plan's signal reasoning rests on a false premise about bash. It says signals run no code and that 'No signal handlers are added ... a signal during the `aws` write leaves the SSM state unknowable from the script', which implies the notice will not fire on a signal. But once a non-interactive bash has an EXIT trap set, it catches the terminating signals (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP) so it can run that trap before dying. With the trap armed across `aws ssm put-parameter`, a Ctrl-C or SIGTERM during the write would print 'SSM was NOT updated', even though the write may already have succeeded. That is the very claim the plan says the script cannot know.
findings.location: Approach — 'No signal handlers are added: ... a signal during the `aws` write leaves the SSM state unknowable from the script'; Root cause — '... or a signal, which runs no code'
scenarios: An operator presses Ctrl-C after AWS has already written the parameter but before `aws` returns. The trap prints 'SSM was NOT updated; the review-bot cannot authenticate', which is false, and the operator re-runs, rotating the token again for no reason.
SIGTERM arrives during the generator call after a successful delete. The notice prints, which is arguably correct, but the plan does not describe or intend this behaviour.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the 'a signal runs no code' claim and state what the EXIT trap prints when the script is killed by a signal, or `aws` fails ambiguously, during the SSM write (where SSM state is unknown), with a test for the signal case.
evidence: Root cause: 'every other way out between the delete and the SSM write is an implicit `set -e` exit or a signal, which runs no code.'
Approach: 'The trap window matches the facts the notice states'
Approach: 'No signal handlers are added: ... a signal during the `aws` write leaves the SSM state unknowable from the script.'

Bash behaviour: on a fatal signal, bash's termination handler runs the EXIT trap. A foreground child is waited on before the deferred signal is acted upon, so the trap fires after `aws` may have completed. This differs from POSIX sh/dash.
findings.finding: The plan assumes signals run no code, but bash runs an EXIT trap when the script is killed by SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP. While the trap is armed, Ctrl-C or SIGTERM during `aws ssm put-parameter` would print the definite claim 'SSM was NOT updated' even if PutParameter already committed. This contradicts the plan's stated rule that the trap window matches the facts the notice states, and its rationale that a signal during the write leaves SSM state unknowable. The same false claim can occur when `aws` exits non-zero after a server-side success, such as a read timeout or a dropped connection after the write applied. The plan states no disposition for these ambiguous arms and no test covers them.
findings.location: Root cause ('a signal, which runs no code') and Approach ('No signal handlers are added ... a signal during the `aws` write leaves the SSM state unknowable')
scenarios: Operator presses Ctrl-C while `aws ssm put-parameter` is in flight and the write completes. The EXIT trap still prints 'SSM was NOT updated; the review-bot cannot authenticate'. The operator re-runs, which deletes and regenerates a token SSM already held correctly, or files a false incident.
`aws` exits 254 on a read timeout after PutParameter was applied. The notice asserts SSM was not updated when its state is actually unknown.
findings.suggested_fix: Track the phase in a variable: set `phase=ssm_write` just before `aws ssm put-parameter`. In the EXIT handler, inspect `$?`. If the exit status is >128 (signal) or phase is `ssm_write` with a non-zero `aws` exit, print an 'SSM state unknown — verify the parameter, or re-run until the script succeeds' variant instead of 'SSM was NOT updated'. Keep the definite notice for failures before the write starts. Add a test that sends SIGTERM to the script while the `aws` stub sleeps, and assert the 'unknown' wording rather than 'NOT updated'.

findings.finding: Arming with `trap '...' EXIT` replaces any EXIT trap already installed, and `trap - EXIT` clears all EXIT handling. The plan mentions only step 5's later cleanup trap. It does not say whether any EXIT trap exists before the delete (e.g. temp-file cleanup), or how the notice would compose with one.
scenarios: An earlier cleanup trap exists. Arming the notice silently drops that cleanup on every path after the delete.

findings.finding: The notice text says "Gerrit's token for '<bot>' was already replaced". The plan also says "The trap window matches the facts the notice states". But in the generator-failure-after-successful-delete case, which the plan explicitly covers, the old token was deleted and no replacement may exist. So the notice states something false for that path.
findings.location: Approach — notice wording vs. the generator-failure case
scenarios: The generator exits 1 after the delete succeeded. The operator reads 'replaced' and may assume a new token exists in Gerrit, when the bot has no `default` token at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Use "Gerrit's token for '<bot>' was already deleted or replaced and SSM was NOT updated; the review-bot cannot authenticate until this script succeeds", and assert on "SSM was NOT" / "cannot authenticate" plus a stable substring that covers both deleted and replaced.
